analysis.one_liner: Restores DEA's ability to suspend drug distributors shipping suspicious opioid orders.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in either committee and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal a 2016 law that made it harder for the Drug Enforcement Administration to suspend drug distributors whose large, suspicious shipments of prescription opioids fed the overdose epidemic. Repealing it would put the older, tougher enforcement rules back in place. The bill was referred to two House committees, sent to their subcommittees, and never acted on before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit by the opioid epidemic, and the DEA's ability to act quickly when a distributor ships orders that are far out of line with legitimate medical need.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Ensuring Patient Access and Effective Drug Enforcement Act of 2016 and restores the Controlled Substances Act provisions as they were before that law was enacted [S2, S3].

The 2016 law replaced DEA's previous standard for suspending a distributor's registration — 'imminent danger to public health' — with a weaker standard requiring both a 'substantial likelihood' of immediate threat and specified Conduct that threatens public health, giving companies a formal notice and comment process before enforcement [S3].
The bill takes effect retroactively, 'as of the enactment' of the 2016 law, so the tougher rules would apply as if the 2016 law had never passed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Drug wholesale distributors and pharmacy chains whose registrations could again be suspended quickly when their shipments look suspicious; communities could see tighter drug supply, including for some legitimate patients.

drawbacks.text: The 2016 law was written to guarantee due process for pharmacies and distributors facing enforcement, including advance notice and an opportunity to comment before sanctions; repealing it retroactively removes those protections for regulated businesses [S3].

Industry and some patient-access advocates argued the old, easier suspension standard risked cutting off legitimate medication supplies to pharmacies serving pain patients; the bill's repeal would restore that harsher standard without any phase-in [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is restoring a fast DEA tool against the distributors that shipped hundreds of millions of pills into communities where overdoses climbed; the main cost is weaker procedural protections for distributors and a possible risk of supply disruption for some legitimate patients. On balance the bill aimed at a clear public-health problem and was written to apply the old rules retroactively, which was aggressive but directly targeted.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees, referred to each committee's health and crime subcommittees, and never came up for a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. William Keating introduced the bill on October 19, 2017, joined by four Democratic cosponsors — Reps. Kuster, Clark, McGovern, and Lynch [S1, S4].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees on the day of introduction, then to the Health subcommittee on October 20 and the Crime subcommittee on November 1 [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote followed; the bill sat in subcommittee until the 115th Congress expired on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug wholesale distributors and pharmacy chains, which continued operating under the 2016 law's weaker enforcement standard rather than facing the faster suspensions this repeal would have restored.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug distributors kept the weaker 2016 rules

for.name: Rep. William R. Keating
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the 2016 enforcement-weakening law and restore the DEA's prior authority.

for.name: Reps. Ann Kuster, Katherine Clark, James McGovern, and Stephen Lynch

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral; the bill went to the Health and Crime subcommittees and never reached a markup or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsor joined, and the Republican-controlled committees never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would strip the 2016 protections that made it much harder for the DEA to suspend their registrations over suspicious opioid shipments, exposing them to faster enforcement. Public interest in controlling pill floods runs against their interest in uninterrupted shipping. [S3]
Reinstating the pre-2016 standard would make suspensions easier to bring against pharmacies dispensing unusually large opioid volumes, a risk for chains serving legitimate patients as well. [S3]
